summary: Near Jerusalem, with the crowd expecting the kingdom at once, Jesus tells of a nobleman who leaves to receive a kingdom and returns to judge his servants and his enemies.
key_insight: The crowd thought the kingdom would appear immediately. Jesus answered with a king who goes to a far country and comes back later. Between the leaving and the return, His servants have one command, “Do business till I come,” while some citizens refuse His reign.
story: As the people listened, Jesus told another parable, because He was near Jerusalem and they thought the kingdom of God would appear immediately.

“A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and to return.” Before he left, he called ten of his servants, gave them ten minas, and said, “Do business till I come.” But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him: “We will not have this man to reign over us.”

He received the kingdom, returned, and called the servants to learn what each had gained. The first said, “Master, your mina has earned ten minas.” “Well done, good servant,” the king said; “because you were faithful in a very little, have authority over ten cities.” The second had earned five minas, and he was set over five cities.

Another came: “Master, here is your mina, which I have kept put away in a handkerchief. For I feared you, because you are an austere man.” He said his master collected what he did not deposit and reaped what he did not sow.

“Out of your own mouth I will judge you, you wicked servant,” the king replied. If the servant believed his master was so hard, why had he not at least put the money in the bank to earn interest? The king ordered the mina taken from him and given to the servant who had ten. “Master, he has ten minas,” they protested. “For I say to you, that to everyone who has will be given; and from him who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.”
Then the king turned to the rebels: “But bring here those enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, and slay them before me.”

fit.question: Luke’s parable of the minas is much like Matthew’s parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30). Is it one parable remembered two different ways?

points.label: Different occasions
points.text: Luke sets the minas near Jericho, before Jesus entered Jerusalem, and says it was told to a crowd that expected the kingdom at once. Matthew sets the talents days later on the Mount of Olives, in private teaching to the disciples.

points.label: Different stories
points.text: In Luke ten servants each receive one mina, a nobleman goes away to receive a kingdom, rebels oppose him, and the rewards are cities. In Matthew three servants receive five talents, two and one, “each according to his own ability,” there are no rebels, and the reward is rule over “many things” and the master’s joy. A talent was worth sixty minas.

points.label: Familiar pictures, new lessons
points.text: Jesus often used similar pictures to teach different things. Here the stress falls on the King’s delay and on rebellion against His reign; in Matthew, on faithful readiness for His return.

fit.note: Similar stories told on different days to different hearers are what we would expect from a teacher who taught for years; nothing here suggests the writers garbled one parable.
fit.short: Two parables on two occasions: the minas near Jericho to a crowd, the talents on the Mount of Olives to the disciples, with different details.

scene.label: A king who went to Rome
scene.text: When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus traveled to Rome to ask Augustus to confirm him as king. A delegation of fifty Jews followed to oppose him. He came back with a lesser title and dealt harshly with his opponents. Archelaus later rebuilt the royal palace at Jericho, near where Jesus told this story.

scene.label: A mina
scene.text: A mina was worth about a hundred denarii, roughly a hundred days’ wages for a laborer. It was a modest sum for a nobleman to entrust to each servant, a test of faithfulness in “a very little.”

scene.label: The bank
scene.text: Luke’s word for bank is the moneychanger’s table, the same word used for the tables Jesus overturned in the temple (Matthew 21:12). Moneychangers and lenders paid interest on money left with them; leaving money with them took no effort at all.

scene.label: Near Jerusalem
scene.text: Jesus was a day’s walk from the city, with Passover crowds around Him and a blind man’s cry of “Son of David” still fresh. Many expected Him to claim the throne as soon as He arrived.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records this parable, and he alone says why Jesus told it: the crowd expected the kingdom at once. It is Jesus’ last teaching before the entry into Jerusalem, where the crowds cry, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the LORD!” (19:38) and the leaders refuse Him, as the citizens in the parable refused their king.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks of Himself as the Nobleman: He would go away to receive His kingdom and come back as King. He knew His people’s leaders would reject His reign, and He knew He would return to settle accounts.
seeing.living: Between His leaving and His return, Jesus has given each servant something to work with and a plain command: “Do business till I come.” Fear that does nothing is not caution; it grows from a false picture of the Master. The faithful put His gifts to work because they trust His character.
seeing.ponder: What has the King placed in your hands, and are you putting it to work or keeping it wrapped up out of fear?

preaching.big_idea: The King has gone and will return; until then, His servants put His gifts to work.
preaching.watch_for: Verse 11 gives the reason for the parable: people thought the kingdom would appear immediately. Even after the resurrection the disciples asked, “Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1:6).
